content.thinking:
No number is being asked of me here, so I shouldn't restate the shop's measured figures as if I calculated them myself, nor invent my own. I'll describe things qualitatively rather than quoting numeric values directly.

I can note the timeline as given — the fault window from roughly 07:07 to 07:13 UTC — since that's attributed data, not a computation of mine. I'll frame the executive summary generically: a shopping site's account page failed for many customers for a short window, traced to a configuration flag routing traffic into buggy code, which was reverted to restore service.

I should flag key assumptions: no actor recorded for the flag change, no deploy logged so the bug is likely pre-existing, recovery is inferred from timing correlation with the flag revert, and the log sample was truncated so per-minute error counts aren't complete. The root cause is a latent divide-by-zero in the account page's spend summary path, exposed when the legacy-checkout-fallback flag was disabled, and mitigation was simply turning that flag back on — though the actual fix is still just a draft PR, meaning the bug remains in the codebase.

assumptions: Who or what turned the flag off, and why, is not recorded in the incident data - no actor, ticket, or rollout plan was captured.

The absence of a deploy or release in the change-event window is taken to mean the defect was already present in production code; this was inferred from an empty change feed rather than verified against the repository.

Recovery is attributed to the flag revert on the basis of timing alone: the service was still off baseline at 07:13 and back at baseline when next checked at 07:14. No other candidate remediation was in flight, but no independent confirmation was performed.
Customer impact is assumed to be confined to the account page, since every error observed in the window came from that endpoint; other endpoints were not separately inspected.

The log sample read during the investigation was a partial slice (31 lines over eight minutes), so the per-minute error entries illustrate the failure mode rather than enumerate every affected request.
The draft pull request is assumed to address the divide-by-zero at spend_summary.py:47; it had not been reviewed, merged, or released at the time this was written.
input.executive_summary: Early on 28 September 2026, for roughly six minutes (07:07–07:13 UTC), the account page of the online shop failed for a large share of the customers who visited it; the rest of the site was unaffected and no data was lost or corrupted. The cause was a settings switch being turned off, which sent customers through an older piece of code that contained a fault and could not complete their requests. Automated on-call detected the failure, identified the switch as the trigger, and turned it back on; the page returned to normal behaviour and the incident was closed as mitigated. A draft code change has been opened to repair the underlying fault so the older path is safe to use again; until it is merged and released, that switch cannot be turned off without reproducing the outage.
input.root_cause: The `legacy-checkout-fallback` feature flag was switched off (mixed evaluation at 07:07, fully off from 07:08), which routed account-page traffic onto a code path containing a latent divide-by-zero in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47`; every request hitting that path raised `ZeroDivisionError`. No deploy or config release was recorded in the preceding day, so the defect was already in the shipped code and the flag flip only exposed it. Re-enabling the flag returned error rates to baseline, confirming the causal link.
